/society/2026/nov/15/no-free-lunch-milbu.headline: Higher training costs for older workers risk plan to tackle youth jobs crisis, employers say
/society/2026/nov/15/no-free-lunch-milbu.excerpt: Britain’s largest employers have told the government that forcing businesses to pay more to train older workers risks damaging its goal to tackle the youth jobs crisis. The Guardian understands ministers plan to overhaul Labour’s apprenticeship funding scheme to increase the cost of training a worker over the age of 25 in England by 25%, to encourage firms to train young people instead. Drawn up before Wednesday’s budget, the proposal, which was first reported last week, is expected to form part of the government response to Alan Milburn’s review into why so many young people are unemployed. The chancellor, John Healey, is widely tipped to announce measures to bolster opportunities for young people to help the 1 million 16- to 24-year-olds not in education, employment or training (Neet) across the country. However, business leaders urged the government to reconsider the plan to make training older workers more expensive. “It will just mean opportunities are shifted around instead of creating new ones,” said Robert Halfon, a former Conservative skills minister who is now the executive director of policy at the manufacturing lobby group Make UK. “We agree that getting young people back into employment and training is a moral and economic imperative. But making it more expensive for employers to train older workers isn’t the answer,” he added.
/society/2026/nov/15/no-free-lunch-milbu.trail: Exclusive: Ministers planning overhaul of apprenticeship funding to increase cost of over-25s training, Guardian understands

/technology/2026/nov/16/ai-related-child.headline: US teens can access ‘nudify’ apps despite Apple and Google’s parental controls, report finds
/technology/2026/nov/16/ai-related-child.excerpt: In December 2025, Morgan Dorfman received distressing news: a student at her daughter’s Pennsylvania high school was making AI-generated pornographic material using the daughter’s image. He was using an artificial intelligence image-editing app called Movely to create sexual videos from pictures of her daughter and five other girls. What Dorfman’s daughter experienced is not an anomaly: students in high schools across the US are reporting similar cases. Their classmates are generating nonconsensual pornographic or nude imagery using so-called “nudify apps”. Governments around the world have moved to ban these AI platforms from app stores, and most US states have implemented laws that criminalize possession of AI-generated child sexual abuse material. However, in spite of regulations prohibiting them, nudification apps are still proliferating and remain accessible to teens, according to a report from the digital advocacy group Tech Transparency Project (TTP) shared exclusively with the Guardian and released on Monday. TTP researchers created four test accounts, two Apple accounts and two Google accounts, indicating the account holders were 13 years old. They searched for image-editing or face-swapping apps using terms such as “AI video generator” or “adult AI”. Using these accounts for a purported 13-year-old, the researchers were able to download 135 apps with features enabling them to strip people of their clothes or swap their faces on to nude bodies.
/technology/2026/nov/16/ai-related-child.trail: Exclusive: Using test accounts, Tech Transparency Project downloaded 135 apps with features to generate nonconsensual nude imagery

/technology/2026/nov/16/ai-related-child.headline: Meta’s legal jeopardy is growing by the day
/technology/2026/nov/16/ai-related-child.excerpt: Hello, and welcome to TechScape. I’m your host, Blake Montgomery, US tech editor at the Guardian. Today in tech, we’re discussing Meta’s legal danger in the US and the implications of artificial intelligence for cybersecurity in an era of private cyber-attacks. Meta finds itself in jeopardy Meta faces a lawsuit from more than half the states in the US, its home country. The trial starts on Tuesday in California. Twenty-nine state attorneys general accuse the company of knowingly designing addictive products that harm the mental health of children. The accusations are similar to a suit brought by an individual earlier this year, a young woman, that the company had negligently operated defective products. She won her case. Another state, New Mexico, brought a suit to trial against Meta earlier this year, accusing the company of knowing of and allowing for child sexual exploitation on its social networks. Meta also lost that case, and a judge imposed a nearly billion-dollar fine over the phases of the trial. The accusations by New Mexico’s attorney general bear less resemblance to Tuesday’s case than the young woman’s, focusing on crimes committed on Facebook rather than damage to a person brought on by their own use of the social network. Meta has denied the accusations in all three cases and plans to appeal both of the losing verdicts. The legal jeopardy that the company faces is severe and growing more so by the day. The states’ legal officials are seeking $200bn in damages.
/technology/2026/nov/16/ai-related-child.trail: Also: AI’s implications on cybersecurity in an era of private attacks

/world/2026/nov/15/women-pardoned-aborti.headline: Reproductive rights protected in several states by midterm election ballot measures
/world/2026/nov/15/women-pardoned-aborti.excerpt: Reproductive rights were on the ballot on Tuesday night as voters weighed in on several abortion-related measures, delivering a largely successful night for reproductive rights advocates encompassed by a historic blue wave. In Nevada, voters approved an amendment enshrining abortion rights in the state constitution, permanently protecting access to abortion through the second trimester after a second referendum on the measure. Question 6, which establishes a “fundamental right to abortion”, was leading 62.3% to 37.7% with 86% of Nevada votes counted when the Associated Press called the race. The amendment allows the state to regulate abortion after viability, except when medically necessary to “protect the life or health of the pregnant patient”. Virginia voters also approved a constitutional amendment establishing a “fundamental right to reproductive freedom”. This measure also protects access to abortion during the first two trimesters of pregnancy. It permits government regulation in the third trimester while preserving access to abortion when necessary to protect the life or health of the pregnant woman. The amendment also establishes rights to contraception and fertility care, among other protections. In Missouri, voters rejected an effort to overturn the constitutional right to reproductive freedom they had approved in 2024.
/world/2026/nov/15/women-pardoned-aborti.trail: Voters in Nevada, Virginia and Missouri passed or strengthened protections for women’s reproductive freedom

/world/2026/nov/15/women-pardoned-aborti.headline: Poland’s parliament votes to ease abortion ban but faces likely veto from president
/world/2026/nov/15/women-pardoned-aborti.excerpt: Poland’s lower house of parliament has approved two bills aimed at loosening a near-total ban on abortions, in what campaigners have described as a “small-scale step” ahead of protests calling on the government to fulfil its promises to overhaul the country’s laws. The new measures, which are likely to be vetoed by Poland’s nationalist president, would remove some of the criminal penalties for those who help women to access abortion care and allow terminations in cases of foetal abnormalities. Leah Hoctor, of the Center for Reproductive Rights, said: “These bills represent a very small-scale change. Even if these pieces of legislation are ratified and signed into law by the Polish president – which remains to be seen – they would change very little for most women in Poland who need abortion care.” This view was echoed by the NGO Legalna Aborcja (Legal Abortion), a reproductive rights and advocacy initiative. “What does this mean for women who need an abortion right now? Nothing, because none of these bills would help them,” said a spokesperson. The Fundacja Widzialne (Visible Foundation) asked people to keep up the pressure on the government by taking to the streets on Thursday. “Poland still has an inhumane abortion law,” it wrote on social media as it announced rallies in 27 cities.
/world/2026/nov/15/women-pardoned-aborti.trail: Measures would remove some penalties for those helping women access abortion but are ‘small-scale step’, say campaigners

/world/2026/nov/15/women-pardoned-aborti.headline: The abortion debate has gone quiet amid US midterms. In Idaho, the stakes remain high
/world/2026/nov/15/women-pardoned-aborti.excerpt: Exactly 1,255 volunteers fanned out across Idaho’s rural 35 legislative districts to collect signatures, knocking on 66,000 doors and ultimately gathering more than 110,000. Not a single one was paid – a rarity in today’s politics. This effort was in service of Proposition 1, which asks voters a single question: Should abortion be legal in Idaho? A “yes” vote would lift one of the most restrictive abortions bans in the nation. “We’re not a large population state – we’re a flyover state, we’re a very red state,” said Melanie Folwell, the lead organizer of the Idahoans United for Women and Families, the group organizing the initiative, “and it’s very easy to forget about a million women and girls.” As Republicans delay major action on abortion until after the election, and Democrats focus on issues like affordability, high-stakes reproductive rights battles have faded from national attention even as they affect millions of women and girls. “It speaks to the very reason we had to run an initiative – because no one was coming to save us in Idaho,” said Folwell. “That is why we wrote an Idaho policy to fix our specific Idaho problem, did it with Idahoans, and funded almost entirely with Idahoans. We raised $3.5m over 6,000 contributions – almost entirely from inside our state.” Four states including Idaho have ballot initiatives that attempt to pin down exactly what kind of landscape they want.
/world/2026/nov/15/women-pardoned-aborti.trail: Republicans delay major action on abortion until after midterm elections, and Democrats focus on affordability

/world/2026/nov/15/women-pardoned-aborti.headline: Victorian Labor makes abortion access easier amid fears One Nation could try to wind it back
/world/2026/nov/15/women-pardoned-aborti.excerpt: The Victorian government is announcing new measures to improve access to medical abortion, as it puts reproductive rights on the election agenda and claims One Nation could use abortion as a negotiating chip with the Coalition in the event of a hung parliament. On Thursday, the deputy premier and minister for women, Gabrielle Williams, and the health minister, Ingrid Stitt, will announce a rollout of new portable ultrasound machines for the state’s 20 sexual and reproductive health hubs. The machines, costing $480,000, will help confirm early pregnancy sooner, making it easier for women, particularly in regional Victoria, to access medical abortion – a drug-induced termination that can be carried out up to nine weeks’ gestation. “It means women, particularly in regional Victoria, will be more likely to be scanned within that nine-week window for medical abortion, rather than having to wait or travel long distances to get a scan, and by then potentially only have surgical abortion options available for them,” Stitt said. Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email Abortion was decriminalised in Victoria in 2008, with women able to obtain a termination during the first 24 weeks of pregnancy, and later if they obtain the agreement of two doctors.

/world/2026/nov/15/women-pardoned-aborti.headline: Baby born via surrogate can leave Texas for treatment in California, court rules
/world/2026/nov/15/women-pardoned-aborti.excerpt: The Texas supreme court has decided that the month-old infant that surrogate McKenna West gave birth to can be relocated to Los Angeles, a Thursday ruling that came weeks after a California court had recognized the biological parents’ custody rights. “Sustaining the life of the medically fragile child is the paramount concern in this time-sensitive matter,” the court wrote in a Thursday order, referring to the baby’s rare severe heart defect. West had attempted to block the biological parents from removing the child from Texas and taking him to a hospital in Los Angeles where the couple live. The court cited testimony from the infant’s Texas physician, who described the window for an ICU-to-ICU transfer as short and “ripe now”. West’s attorneys did not immediately respond to a request for comment about the Thursday ruling. The infant, named Rumi by his biological parents, has hypoplastic left heart syndrome, a condition that impedes blood flow and requires extensive surgery. Without treatment, the defect can be fatal. The condition was detected when the baby was a fetus, prompting California couple Nausheen Gilkar and Omar Ahmed to reportedly ask that West terminate the pregnancy. West, who resides in Alaska, traveled to Texas, where abortion is illegal, to deliver the child.
/world/2026/nov/15/women-pardoned-aborti.trail: Ruling latest step in legal fight over medically fragile child born after surrogate reportedly rejected couple’s request for abortion

The Singapore-based cloud computing company on the weekend said it was “aware of recent media reports containing assertions about our business, supply chain and global operations that are not supported by verifiable evidence”. Megaspeed said it had “retained external legal counsel to conduct a thorough internal investigation”. Jensen Huang resigned as chief executive of the chip manufacturer Nvidia after reports of extramarital affairs with Alice Huang and two company employees. US intelligence agencies believe the tech chief, whose products have been crucial to the AI boom, had been targeted by Alice Huang, the former director of Megaspeed International. In the past three years, Megaspeed has been one of Nvidia’s biggest foreign customers, buying nearly US$5bn (A$7.4bn, £3.8bn) in AI chips and advanced hardware. Megaspeed said on Sunday it would not comment on Alice Huang’s “personal and private matters”.

/technology/2026/nov/16/elon-musk-tech-e.headline: Trump bought Nvidia stock as he helped chipmaker with change to export rule
/technology/2026/nov/16/elon-musk-tech-e.excerpt: Donald Trump bought Nvidia stock worth millions of dollars as he made decisions on America’s China policy that would benefit the chipmaker, an analysis has found. In May 2025, Trump’s administration rescinded a Biden-era rule designed to prevent the most advanced US-made AI chips from being exported to China. This rule aimed to strengthen the US’s own chip industry and to protect America from what was widely regarded as a national security threat: the possibility that China might develop superior AI. In the days before he rescinded the rule, Trump’s public financial disclosures indicate that he bought between $1m (£760,000) and $5m worth of Nvidia stock – a purchase noted in an analysis by the anti-corruption group DeKleptocracy. He also bought shares in other tech companies, including Apple, Meta and Microsoft. The diffusion rule would have limited Nvidia’s ability to sell to what has been one of its largest markets: China accounted for about a quarter of the company’s sales between 2010 and 2022. Nvidia’s shares rose in value just after Trump announced the rescission of the rule, and after he had bought the stock. In December 2025 Trump said he would allow Nvidia to sell H200 chips to China, a decision that was greenlit by the Department of Commerce in January 2026. This was a controversial move. H200s were one of the company’s most advanced chips – six times better than what was available in China at the time, said experts.
/technology/2026/nov/16/elon-musk-tech-e.trail: President purchased up to $5m of stock before revoking Biden-era rule that limited Nvidia’s ability to sell to China

/technology/2026/nov/16/elon-musk-tech-e.headline: A timeline of the affair scandal that sank Nvidia’s Jensen Huang
/technology/2026/nov/16/elon-musk-tech-e.excerpt: Jensen Huang has stepped down as CEO of Nvidia, the company at the center of the AI boom, after leading it for more than 30 years. Huang, an electrical engineer by education, stewarded the company from a $1bn firm when it went public in 1999 to a company valued at more than $4tn in 2026. But in a matter of days, after it was revealed he had an extramarital affair with a woman that US officials believe to be a Chinese spy, Huang managed to wipe more than $600bn from the company’s valuation. China has denied the accusations that it had tapped Alice Huang, the woman in question and a top executive at a datacenter company called Megaspeed, to be an intelligence asset, and called them a “smear”. US officials had reportedly started to monitor the Megaspeed executive after suspecting the firm was diverting powerful Nvidia AI chips to Chinese firms, in potential violation of export restrictions. The Biden and Trump administrations had prohibited US companies from exporting some of the more powerful AI chips to China over national security concerns. Just a week ago it seemed that Huang’s ouster was unlikely, but in the days since he first disclosed an affair and affirmed his commitment to the company, the New York Times reported that there was a second affair – this time with another Nvidia executive. A lot has happened in the last few days, but how did we get here? Here’s a timeline of what we know about Huang’s entanglements.

/technology/2026/nov/16/elon-musk-tech-e.headline: Who is Colette Kress, interim Nvidia CEO after Jensen Huang exit?
/technology/2026/nov/16/elon-musk-tech-e.excerpt: The hunt is on for a new Nvidia CEO. It comes after a whirlwind week, which saw the company head and co-founder, Jensen Huang, resign amid multiple allegations of extramarital affairs, including one that involved an alleged Chinese spy and two with company employees. Nvidia immediately named Colette Kress, the company’s chief financial officer, as the interim CEO. It’s possible she could stay on permanently, but the company could also name another candidate for the full-time role. Names that have been floated include Ian Buck, who manages Nvidia’s AI hardware and software products, and Rene Haas, a former Nvidia employee and the current CEO of Arm Holdings, a UK-based chipmaker. Whoever takes over from Huang will have tremendous sway in the burgeoning world of artificial intelligence. The entire AI ecosphere relies on Nvidia, which engineers advanced chips used to train AI models and power companies such as OpenAI, Anthropic and Google. Nvidia is also a central driver of the US economy and one of the world’s most valuable companies, with a market cap of around $4tn. Huang, who co-founded the company in 1993, is known as an ambitious and visionary CEO who had a hand in most all aspects of the business. He led in an unusual management style, having about 60 direct reports, giving him more control over the company’s daily functions.
/technology/2026/nov/16/elon-musk-tech-e.trail: Chief financial officer, reportedly disparaged by Huang during summer meeting, to take over on short-term basis

/sport/2026/nov/16/lewis-hamilton-urges-.headline: Dominant Lando Norris powers to victory in São Paulo F1 Grand Prix
/sport/2026/nov/16/lewis-hamilton-urges-.excerpt: Lando Norris delivered a masterclass for victory at the São Paulo Grand Prix, taking the flag at a meeting marked by a series of striking comebacks. Max Verstappen was once more outstanding at Interlagos by taking second from 21st on the grid and for McLaren it was a victory they have sought since mid-season. But of most import was confirmation of a definitive return from the wilderness for Mercedes as they claimed their ninth Formula One constructors’ world championship. What it meant to Mercedes was clear, with as many of the team personnel as could be squeezed on to the podium in São Paulo celebrating the achievement. The drivers – the newly crowned world champion, Kimi Antonelli, and George Russell – and the team principal, Toto Wolff, sportingly allowed them their moment before joining them to share in the redemptive joy. With it Mercedes have sealed their first drivers’ and constructors’ double since Lewis Hamilton last took the drivers’ title in 2020, and their first constructors’ championship at all since 2021. They needed to outscore second-placed Ferrari by three points in Brazil; Antonelli finishing fifth and Russell fourth proved more than enough. The feat is even more impressive given how much Mercedes struggled under the last set of regulations. They endured four long years of battering away to little effect, a drought from which there was no guarantee they could return to winning ways.
/sport/2026/nov/16/lewis-hamilton-urges-.trail: Lando Norris won the Sao Paulo Grand Prix while Mercedes sealed victory in the constructors’ championship

/sport/2026/nov/16/lewis-hamilton-urges-.headline: Lando Norris claims F1 São Paulo GP pole as ‘crazy’ rain disrupts qualifying
/sport/2026/nov/16/lewis-hamilton-urges-.excerpt: Mastering the most treacherous of conditions at Interlagos, Lando Norris had the edge to take pole position for McLaren at the São Paulo Grand Prix, having bested a downpour that tested every driver. But with more rain predicted for the race on Sunday, it remains wide open from the front to the very back of the grid. After a qualifying session that took two and a half hours to complete because of delays caused by the heavy rain, Norris came out on top but the grid will be marked by a very mixed-up formation, as a host of drivers took penalties. “We could just have an exciting race with a little bit of everything, honestly,” he said. “I was certainly more confident in the wet and inter [intermediate] than I was in the dry. I think in the dry we just didn’t have the pace, so I’ll be certainly more happy if I wake up and see rain in the morning.” Mercedes’ George Russell was second on track but the British driver has a grid penalty, promoting his teammate Kimi Antonelli, the new world champion, to second and Racing Bulls’ Liam Lawson to third, with Audi’s Nico Hülkenberg up to fourth. Interlagos was awash with streams of water flooding across the track so the early runs were a real test. Russell called the conditions “crazy”. “I love driving in the rain. I love driving in the rain here but if that was a race there was no way we should be driving in that,” he said.

However, after Hamilton and his teammate Charles Leclerc clashed at the Autódromo Hermanos Rodríguez, the Briton clearly believes that a title tilt in 2027 might be at risk, as the team apparently vacillate on how to manage having two No 1 drivers, both determined to be the top dog around which Ferrari should coalesce. /sport/2026/nov/16/lewis-hamilton-urges-.headline: Lewis Hamilton refuses to back down over criticism of teammate Leclerc
/sport/2026/nov/16/lewis-hamilton-urges-.excerpt: Lewis Hamilton has refused to back down over his criticism of his Ferrari teammate Charles Leclerc after a flashpoint between the pair at last weekend’s Mexico Grand Prix. Leclerc and Hamilton were competing with one another at turn four on the opening lap of the race in Mexico last Sunday, with Leclerc attempting to pass his teammate. He went off in doing so and Hamilton’s defence left him vulnerable to being passed by Max Verstappen who went on to win, costing Ferrari a potential one-two. Ferrari do not have formal rules of engagement between their drivers and Hamilton said at the time that the team had “big, big problems”, later squarely blaming his teammate for costing them a shot at victory. “The guy is 29 years old, so I don’t think it’s an age thing. Speaking before this weekend’s São Paulo Grand Prix Hamilton was insistent he would not back down from his remarks. “I don’t really care what everyone thinks about what I said, I wear my heart on my sleeve and I say how I feel in the moment,” he said. “Of course there’s times you say things and maybe you might regret it afterwards. I don’t. “I’m never going to apologise for being authentic and real and I’m not going to be silenced.

/law/2026/nov/15/uk-government-to-consid.headline: Is it finally OK to be frank about 2000s pop culture? ‘It was profoundly, cheerfully horrible to women’
/law/2026/nov/15/uk-government-to-consid.excerpt: In a 2008 episode of BBC Two’s comedy panel show Never Mind the Buzzcocks, the choreographer Arlene Phillips – the only woman on the programme – was told by the host Simon Amstell: “You look like you run a good whore house.” In reply, Phillips told a story with what appeared to be faux sincerity: while working with big stars, she explained, she would sometimes be asked to find dancers with “very special abilities” who might want to party after filming. Another panellist, the TV presenter Dermot O’Leary, mimed picking up a phone and said: “When you’re dancing tonight, do you mind having sex afterwards?” Everyone laughed. Russell Brand’s imprisonment for rape and sexual assault this week, and allegations of sexual misconduct against the comedian and children’s author David Walliams have prompted scrutiny not only of the men involved, but of those who appeared to enable them. The chatshow host Jonathan Ross has apologised for a 2004 joke, in which he described the 15-year-old British comedy awards as being “like most 15-year-olds: drunk, unpredictable and probably going home with David Walliams”. The latter has denied the allegations made against him in reporting by the Guardian and ITV News, but is now the focus of an investigation by the Met police on separate sexual misconduct claims. On the face of it, Phillips’s story had nothing to do with Brand or Walliams. But as clips like this have resurfaced they have been viewed in a different light.

/law/2026/nov/15/uk-government-to-consid.headline: Two courtrooms, one celebrity: how did the Russell Brand case compare with the rape trial next door?
/law/2026/nov/15/uk-government-to-consid.excerpt: What is going on inside Russell Brand’s head as he arrives at court for the start of his rape trial? He sees the dozens of cameras and journalists lined outside Southwark crown court, many of whom have been waiting since before 7am, and he tells himself that the media are all against him. “It seems to me that they believe that I am guilty, and that this should be the rubber-stamping of the process of my destruction.” He walks with his wife, Laura, and his bodyguard past the photographers, “clickering, clackering, snickering paparazzi, like locusts, peculiar concoctions, not fully humans”, and up into the court, where he is suddenly overwhelmed by “the presence of something very beautiful, grace”. “In a situation like I’m in, it’s impossible not to turn to God. Truth and justice are the only things that can save me,” he thinks. In one of the early hearings, he also receives some words of support from a court security guard, “just some normal geezer, patting me down for weapons or sharps”, who whispers: “All right, Russell. The whole country’s behind you, mate. The whole country’s behind you.” Brand takes solace from these words. “I felt very, very encouraged.” I’m not a mind reader, so how do I know all this? Usually we know nothing about the thoughts of defendants in trials because they stay silent for the duration, but Brand finds it hard to stay quiet.
/law/2026/nov/15/uk-government-to-consid.trail: One was a high-profile defendant watched by more than 100 journalists. Another was an unknown man who preyed on a girl almost half his age. Their stories played out minutes apart, one entirely out of the spotlight

/law/2026/nov/15/uk-government-to-consid.headline: ‘I felt sick at the sight of him parading around’: Russell Brand’s victims on the lifelong impact of his crimes
/law/2026/nov/15/uk-government-to-consid.excerpt: Victims of Russell Brand have described the lasting impact of his crimes in statements read out at Southwark crown court by the prosecutor, Riel Karmy-Jones, on Monday. Here are the abbreviated words of the four women, one of whom read out her own statement from behind a screen. ‘I literally lost any love for myself’ The woman was sexually assaulted at a birthday party in Soho, London, in 2004, with Brand grabbing her breasts. She read out her own statement, saying: When it happened I was in complete shock and turmoil for weeks trying to process what had happened to me, I was extremely upset and traumatised. It really affected how I viewed myself, I didn’t have any respect for myself and got into situations with toxic men as I didn’t have any self-worth. I literally lost any love for myself for a long time, thinking that I was damaged goods. I felt vulnerable whenever I was going for an evening out for a long time after it happened, scared of giving off any signals that could be taken the wrong way. That undeserved feeling of shame and ‘what if I’d done this or done that’ has been carried around inside me for over 20 years, always there even when I’ve tried to compartmentalise and get on with my life. For many years, as his star was rising, it was impossible to escape seeing him all over the media, being celebrated for his disgusting behaviour against women like it was all a joke.

/uk-news/2026/nov/15/prince-harry-ukrain.headline: Uganda reverses Invictus Games withdrawal after reassurance from King Charles
/uk-news/2026/nov/15/prince-harry-ukrain.excerpt: Uganda has U-turned on its decision to withdraw from the Duke of Sussex’s Invictus Games after the country’s military chief said he had been reassured by King Charles that there was “no problem” with its participation. Last week, Gen Muhoozi Kainerugaba, the eldest son of the Ugandan president, Yoweri Museveni, made the surprise announcement the country would not participate in the games in a post on X. He said he was motivated by his respect for the king amid division over the “Harry-Meghan nonsense”. However, a post on Monday from the spokesperson of the Uganda People’s Defence Force (UPDF), Chris Magezi, announced that Kainerugaba had reinstated Uganda’s participation in the 2027 Invictus Games, which will be held in Birmingham. Magezi wrote that the shift was prompted by a telephone conversation between Kainerugaba and the principal private secretary to the king and queen, Clive Alderton. Alderton had “revealed that King Charles III was moved by Gen Kainerugaba’s sensitive consideration of the king’s opinion on the upcoming Invictus Games organised by Prince Harry, the Duke of Sussex”. He added that Charles “has no problem with Uganda’s participation in the Invictus Games, and encouraged the [Chief of Defence Forces] CDF to proceed with preparations”. Kainerugaba “appreciated the king’s message and clarity provided by Buckingham Palace on the subject, promising that the UPDF would resume preparations to participate in the upcoming games”.
/uk-news/2026/nov/15/prince-harry-ukrain.trail: Military chief had pulled country out over ‘Harry-Meghan nonsense’ but U-turned after clarification from the palace

/uk-news/2026/nov/15/prince-harry-ukrain.headline: Uganda to withdraw from Invictus Games ‘out of respect for King Charles’, says military chief
/uk-news/2026/nov/15/prince-harry-ukrain.excerpt: Uganda is withdrawing from the Duke of Sussex’s Invictus Games, the country’s military chief has said, out of respect for King Charles amid division over the “Harry-Meghan nonsense”. Gen Muhoozi Kainerugaba, son of the Ugandan president, made the surprise announcement in a post on X on Wednesday. Kainerugaba wrote: “In order not to be construed as being opposed to His Majesty King Charles III of the United Kingdom, whom we deeply revere, Uganda hereby withdraws from the Invictus Games. We shall not participate in anything that does not have His Majesty’s approval.” The timing of the post suggests it may be in response to an official letter to UK senior government and military officials on behalf of Charles that reiterated the Duke and Duchess of Sussex were not working royals and would not use their HRH styles. When asked by the Times about what had motivated the move, Kainerugaba is reported to have said: “I have factions in the Ministry of Defence that support that Harry-Meghan nonsense. I had to quash it straight away. I support the monarch. Period.” The news, first reported by the Uganda Pulse news website, will be a blow to Harry, who two months ago stood alongside Uganda’s defence minister, Kiryowa Kiwanuka, at an Invictus Games event in London to announce that the East African nation would be the 26th country to enter the multisport event for wounded service personnel.

/stage/2026/nov/16/stage-version-tv-seri.headline: This extraordinary new Hamlet turns Shakespeare inside out with infinite jest – and cuddly toys
/stage/2026/nov/16/stage-version-tv-seri.excerpt: Hamlet is trying to get a hire car. He has missed his dad’s funeral because he was at a silent retreat, dealing with his abandonment issues and the disturbing memory of a year 7 disco when his uncle and mum danced together to Yazoo’s Only You. There have been many takes on the troubled Prince of Denmark, but performer/director Ben Duke, co-founder of Lost Dog, has a talent for fresh readings. If Duke has a shtick – which after similar reworkings of Paradise Lost, Romeo and Juliet and the Medea myth, you could argue he does – it is to turn old texts inside out and douse them in contemporary references, surreal swerves and witty one-liners. A formula of sorts, but one that’s wholly unpredictable. Some people think there have already been too many Hamlets. This show starts with an interview director Katie Mitchell gave to Radio 4 earlier this year, appealing for a moratorium on Hamlet, saying she is “tired of plays about depressed, angry, misogynistic men”. Duke’s onstage alter ego, nevertheless, is going to give it one more shot, except due to budget constraints, he’s had to replace the other actors with cuddly toys. He pulls a giant fluffy goose out of a cardboard box to play his mother, Gertrude, and finds his uncle Claudius (a snake) in there, too.
/stage/2026/nov/16/stage-version-tv-seri.trail: Ben Duke’s clever, witty and wholly unpredictable new show, The Last Hamlet, takes big liberties with the story that pay off

/stage/2026/nov/16/stage-version-tv-seri.headline: ‘Turner prize for dance’ winner Christos Papadopoulos: failure, friction and my forgotten youthquake
/stage/2026/nov/16/stage-version-tv-seri.excerpt: Christos Papadopoulos is talking about how to spend £40,000. Specifically the winnings he scooped from the first ever Rose international prize for choreography in 2025 – the dance world’s equivalent of the Turner and the Booker. The Greek choreographer came out top of four finalists, picked by a judging panel including Arlene Phillips and PJ Harvey, for his piece Larsen C, a shadowy, trance-like and glacially paced crescendo of a dance named after an Antarctic ice shelf. Forty grand is not a bad bounty. Did he blow it on designer gear and exotic holidays? He did not. A big chunk went to his dancers, “because they are very hardworking and not so well paid – that’s the Greek reality”. The rest he invested in his new production: “I had some holes to fill, you know, in the budget.” The win may not have made Papadopoulos a household name (this is contemporary dance we’re talking about), but his work is touring worldwide. We speak over video call from Shanghai, where he is performing My Fierce Ignorant Step before its UK premiere. The title, he admits, is a bit weird. It came to him before he’d started making the dance and refers to Papadopoulos’s younger self, full of naive optimism, youthful hope and revolutionary zeal to change the world. Growing up in a small town in the Peloponnese, Papadopoulos spent much of his time in nature. In the summer, he would be out all day “just wandering the mountains and playing”.
/stage/2026/nov/16/stage-version-tv-seri.trail: Amid galloping global crises, the Greek choreographer has returned to his revolutionary ideals. He explains how asking the near-impossible of dancers brings a shared joy

/stage/2026/nov/16/stage-version-tv-seri.headline: The best theatre to stream this month: the Gisèle Pelicot trial becomes an all-star play that ‘just floors you’
/stage/2026/nov/16/stage-version-tv-seri.excerpt: The Pelicot Trial Swiss director Milo Rau’s ripped-from-the-headlines approach to theatre has included shows about wars in Iraq and Congo and the exploitation of migrant workers. His four-hour documentary play (created with Servane Dècle) about the trial of the men who drugged and raped Gisèle Pelicot has been performed around the world and will be staged by the Young Vic at London’s County Hall on 30 November. The production swiftly sold out but will be livestreamed in full. The cast includes Adjoa Andoh, Rosie Jones and Olivia Williams. “It was the act of witnessing that really got me,” said Young Vic boss Nadia Fall of the show. “It isn’t scenes and costumes in a set like a traditional piece of theatre. It is the facts. It just floors you.” ITA Music Vol 1: New Originals It’s already one of Europe’s coolest theatre companies, an avant garde hit factory that stormed the West End with The Years and Oedipus. Now, Internationaal Theater Amsterdam has launched its own record label to release the “most requested” music from its recent productions. The first compilation includes tracks by Thijs van Vuure from an adaptation of James Baldwin’s novel Giovanni’s Room. Available on Spotify. DuEls The moving mosaic of schoolboys he painstakingly choreographed for the viral Storm video has brought Damien Jalet on to the smartphones of a huge new audience.
/stage/2026/nov/16/stage-version-tv-seri.trail: An unmissable documentary play, Tom Stoppard’s Arcadia with luminous Isis Hainsworth and ecstatic dance in a Norwegian museum are among November’s highlights
